Click a number for the longest win on that board, on the large board; ‹ › step through the win and ▶︎ plays it to the end.

The green numbers on the diagonal W − H = H − 1, that is W = 2H − 1, are no coincidence: on those boards a general trapping mechanism works, the V, with which three kings win on every board size (for odd H from 9 on only with playable corner squares). Likewise the columns W − H = 1 and 2 are the families W = H + 1 and H + 2, each with its own trapping position. How they work is shown at the trapping positions.

In the tables: 21 = won, longest win 21 plies · 21* = won provided the stronger side occupies the long diagonal(s) · (21) = drawn (the number is the longest win among the positions that are won) · 13/15 = unplayable/playable corner squares. A board W × H is width × height, with W ≥ H; the tables have a row for every H and a column for every W − H. Playable = the corner squares are playable, unplayable = they are not (only relevant for odd × odd). † : on 8×8 there are 40 positions (2 up to symmetry) with the single king to move that draw by a fork, even with white on the long diagonal.

The 10×10 numbers agree with the statistics of mdgsoftware.nl: with three kings to move 486,444 wins and 434,756 draws (3 against 1); with the single king to move 16,812 wins, 863,802 draws and 40,586 losses (1 against 3).

The three families

FamilyResult (H = 3 … 12)
W = H + 1won on every board
W = H + 2won, except the "wrong" colouring, unplayable corner squares, for H = 9 and 11
W = 2H − 1won, except unplayable for H = 9 and 11 (19×10: 27 plies, 21×11 playable corners: 25 plies, 23×12: 27 plies)

The colouring rule of the book is confirmed: from H = 9 on, for odd H only the colouring with playable corner squares wins. Up to H = 7 the wrong colouring still wins (9×5 and 13×7 unplayable corners) because the general method still reaches that far. How the families win is shown with the trapping positions.

The general method on narrow boards

  • H = 5, 6: every non-square board is won (checked up to 16×5 and 17×6). Three kings in a column close off the full width and can be pushed along the board; the longest win grows by about 2 plies per extra column.
  • H = 7:
    • the three families: W = 8, 9 and 13, won with both colourings;
    • W = 7 (with playable corners provided the long diagonal is held), 10 and 11: already known from the book;
    • W = 12, 14 and 15 (playable corners): new findings. The longest wins jump from 25 to 35, 53 and 67 plies;
    • W ≥ 16: drawn.
  • H = 8:
    • the three families: W = 9, 10 and 15;
    • W = 8 (with the long diagonal) and 11: already known;
    • W ≥ 12, except 15: drawn.
  • H ≥ 9: only the families remain.

The form of the analyses is taken from those by Wieger Wesselink on 10x10.org.

Click a move to see the position on the large board; ‹ › (or the arrow keys) step through the line, ⏮︎ ⏭︎ jump to its start and end, ▶︎ plays it. Values are for the side to move; for a move, for the side making it, with n the number of plies to the end of the game, the move included: W = win (odd), L = loss (even), D = draw. Blue = main line, green = side line, italics = continuation by the database, ? = a move that changes the result according to the database, with the better move or the refutation in [ ] (≡ = back to the position before that move), * = the only move that keeps the win or the draw. The # button turns the square names on the large board on or off; the button with the range of the square names (e.g. 1…18 or a1…f6 on 6×6) switches between numeric and algebraic notation, in the text as well.
